e.etymology: Jean and Marie written as one word. In French Jean-Marie is a man's name, John with Mary added in devotion; in mid-century America Jeanmarie was mostly given to girls, with the English Jean.
A spelling of Shanice, an African-American coinage that joins the Sha- opening to the ending of Janice. It peaked just after the singer Shanice's 1991 hit I Love Your Smile.
A variant of Elwood, an English surname from a place name generally explained as Old English for elder tree wood.
An American name of the early 1900s that pairs the Del- of Delbert and Delmar with the -win ending of Edwin and Alwin.
A surname and 1980s first name treated as a variant of Darrell, the Norman surname d'Airelle, from the village of Airelle in Normandy.
A respelling of Elijah, from Hebrew Eliyahu, my God is Yahweh. Elijah is the prophet of the Books of Kings who is carried to heaven in a chariot of fire.
The job title given as a first name. In the 1800s some American parents named sons with words of rank and profession, such as Lawyer, Judge, Doctor and Major.
A pet form of Elizabeth and Elisabeth, from Hebrew Elisheva, my God is an oath. It was given as a full name in the US in the late 1800s.
A spelling of Darwin, an English surname from the Old English personal name Deorwine, which joins deor (dear) and wine (friend).
A mid-20th-century spelling of Patty, the pet form of Patricia, from Latin patricius, a patrician or member of the Roman nobility.
namesakes: Patti Smith (punk rock singer and poet)

e.etymology: The French feminine form of Ernest, from the Germanic word ernust, serious or earnest.
namesakes: Ernestine (Lily Tomlin's telephone operator on Laugh-In)

e.etymology: The short form of Douglas, the Scottish clan name from Gaelic dubh (black, dark) and glais (stream). Doug was registered as a full name mainly in the 1950s and 1960s.
namesakes: Doug Funnie (title character of the 1990s cartoon Doug)

e.etymology: A pet form of Pearl, the gem name that came into fashion in the late 1800s. The word pearl reached English from Old French perle.
A mid-century name close to Deanna and Diane, often written DeAnne as if Dee plus Anne. Some families use it as a feminine form of Dean.
An American elaboration of Vern, the short form of Vernon, with the -ell ending of Darnell and Wardell. It has been given to both boys and girls.
An old English pet form of Ann, later also used for Nancy, which itself began as a pet form of Ann. Ann comes from the Hebrew name Hannah, grace or favor.
e.note: In British English nan is an everyday word for grandmother.

e.etymology: An African-American name of the 1970s made by adding the La- prefix to Tanya, the Russian pet form of Tatiana.
A German short form of Ernesta and Ernestine, feminine forms of Ernst, from Old High German ernust, serious or earnest. An Old Norse Erna, wife of Jarl in the poem Rigsthula, has the same form.
An English surname from places named for a river crossing beside a mill, mill plus ford.
As a surname Ardis is a reduced form of the Scottish Allardice. The girls' name of the 1920s sits beside Ardith and Ardys; how the surname and the first name are connected is not recorded.
The Latin Bible's spelling of Orpah, the sister-in-law of Ruth who turns back to Moab. The Hebrew name is traditionally explained as nape of the neck, for her turning away.
A phonetic spelling of Felicia, from Latin felicia, happy things or happy times, built on felix, fortunate. Felicia is the feminine counterpart of Felix.

assoc.t: Bye, Felicia, a dismissive catchphrase from the film Friday

e.note: Bye, Felicia, a line from the 1995 film Friday, is a common way to wave someone off.

e.etymology: A respelling of Sybil, from Greek Sibylla, the title of the prophetesses of the ancient world who spoke oracles.
A short form of Frances, Francine and Francis, from Latin Franciscus, Frenchman, the byname of Saint Francis of Assisi. In Spanish and Croatian, Fran is a man's name, short for Francisco or Franjo.
From a French surname, taken up as a first name in honor of the dancer and film star Cyd Charisse. It is often associated with Greek charis, grace, though the surname's own source is unclear.
A Latinate form of Jeanette, the French diminutive of Jeanne, the feminine of Jean (John). John comes from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious.
A variant of Darlene, a 20th-century coinage from the word darling, shaped like Charlene and Marlene.
The feminine form of Aldo, an Italian name from the Germanic element ald, old and so experienced or wise.

assoc.t: Alan Alda, star of the TV series MASH

e.etymology: A mid-century American blend of Geraldine, or its short form Geri, with the -lyn ending.
A spelling of Carlton, an English surname from the many places named with Old English ceorl or Old Norse karl (free man, peasant) and tun (settlement).
A respelling of Jeremy, the medieval English form of Jeremiah, from Hebrew Yirmeyahu, the Lord will exalt. The spelling leans on Jerome, an unrelated Greek name.
